content: Before initiating therapy with Maxipime (cefepime) for injection, it is essential to conduct a thorough assessment of the patient’s medical history to determine if they have experienced any prior immediate hypersensitivity reactions to cefepime, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Caution should be exercised when administering this medication to patients with a known sensitivity to penicillin, as cross-hypersensitivity among beta-lactam antibiotics has been well-documented and may occur in up to 10% of individuals with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction to Maxipime occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately. In patients with renal impairment, defined as a creatinine clearance of 60 mL/min or less, the dosage of Maxipime (cefepime hydrochloride) must be adjusted to account for the reduced rate of renal elimination. Failure to adjust the dosage in such patients can result in elevated and prolonged serum concentrations of cefepime, which may lead to toxicity. The appropriate dosage should be determined based on the degree of renal impairment, the severity of the infection, and the susceptibility of the causative organisms. Serious adverse reactions, including life-threatening or fatal neurotoxicity, have been reported during postmarketing surveillance of cefepime. These reactions include encephalopathy (manifesting as confusion, hallucinations, stupor, or coma), myoclonus, seizures, and nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Most cases of neurotoxicity have occurred in patients with renal impairment who did not receive appropriate dosage adjustments. However, neurotoxicity has also been reported in some patients who were receiving adjusted dosages based on their renal function. In the majority of cases, symptoms of neurotoxicity were reversible and resolved after discontinuation of cefepime and/or following hemodialysis. If neurotoxicity associated with cefepime therapy is suspected, discontinuation of the drug or further dosage adjustments should be considered, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Maxipime, and can range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. The use of antibacterial agents alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and may necessitate colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A detailed medical history is crucial, as CDAD has been reported to occur up to two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate management should include fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation when clinically indicated.
